summary:
Article 296 of the Penal Code (Law 11/2004) punishes sodomy with one to three years' imprisonment, and the provision applies to Muslims and non-Muslims alike; sexual acts between women are also criminalised on the same three-year maximum. It replaced Article 201 of the 1971 Penal Code, which had carried up to five years, and that provision in turn descended from Article 171 of the 1956 code and from the Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938. For Muslims duly convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility, though it has never been imposed. The state does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation between same-gender partners is itself illegal.

Transgender people face a distinct detention power: they may be held for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions. Reporting sourced to the BBC states that trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while in custody, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release; Qatari authorities categorically rejected those allegations. Human Rights Watch documented arrests in public places on the sole basis of gender expression, accompanied by unlawful searches.

Detentions and prosecutions have reached visitors as well as residents. On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile, held for 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer; the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment, including that detainees in that case were denied antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV. A 1998 American visitor was sentenced to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity, and in 2016 a Polish Instagram star spent two months in custody on suspicion of being homosexual. In May 2023 a Qatar Airways employee was detained by the Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution; an officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation, and reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar after mass arrests and deportations.

Police abuse of LGBT people is documented across the 2019 to 2022 period, including beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". Human Rights Watch reported on 24 October 2022 six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody, with mistreatment recorded as recently as September 2022 as Qatar prepared to host the 2022 World Cup under global scrutiny. A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to come out publicly as gay, described LGBTQ people being held and physically abused and then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to become informants against others. The government does not allow people in Qatar to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and in 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law.

Official statements on entry and conduct are conditional rather than protective. In May 2022 the Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture, and in 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans, and Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon". Some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright in May 2022, while others accepted them only if they hid their relationship in public. In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country and the bloc agreed to discuss it, then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting.
tangentialFactors:
Qatar voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the Human Rights Council in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025, positioning the state in sustained opposition to the international monitoring mechanism most relevant to these abuses. The Australian men's national team publicly called in October 2022 for Qatar to recognise same-sex marriage.

Censorship is a documented feature of the domestic environment. In 2018 nine articles on gay and transgender rights were cut from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition, prompting the Government Communications Office to pledge an investigation. In June 2019 the state-linked outlet AJ+ marked LGBTQ Pride Month, drawing criticism for the contrast with domestic censorship, and in 2022 Transport for London banned Qatari advertising after Qatar moved to block rainbow armbands, with Qatar subsequently reviewing its London investments. A 2016 Doha News opinion piece by a gay Qatari man writing as "Majid Al-Qatari" drew extremely strong reactions for allowing the topic to be discussed, and the 2018 reporting on the taboo described a Qatari's account of irreparable damage to mental health.

For comparison, the neighbouring Gulf states share the regional legal frame in which the 2013 entry-ban proposal originated; Qatar is the one jurisdiction in that group whose hosting of a global sporting event drew the sustained external scrutiny recorded in these sources.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the Article 296 maximum of three years and under the six-month no-charge detention power for suspected gender non-conformity, with no statutory mechanism for legal gender recognition described in the sources. Forced detransition and mandated conversion "therapy" are reported as conditions of custody and release for trans detainees.

Campaigning for LGBTQ rights inside Qatar is prohibited, and protesters criticising Qatari law were arrested in 2022. Co-habitation by same-gender partners is illegal, and no recognition of marriage, civil unions or partnerships exists. Coercion of detainees into informing on other LGBT people was described in a May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed. Migrant workers from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand are reported to face particular targeting in appearance-based enforcement; a Qatar Airways employee was detained in May 2023 over cosmetics and clothing, then deported, dismissed and banned. The Philippine Overseas Employment Administration barred gay Philippine workers from Qatar in the 1990s after mass arrests and deportations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not establish how often Article 296 is currently prosecuted, and no case in the inventory shows a completed criminal trial under that article after 1998; the capital sharia penalty is described as theoretical and never imposed, so its practical reach is unresolved. Whether the entrapment-style online policing recorded in February 2024 has continued after that case is not sourced.

The forced-detransition and conversion-therapy allegations are attributed to BBC-sourced reporting that Qatari authorities categorically rejected; the inventory carries no independent verification or government rebuttal beyond that rejection, so the scope of the practice remains contested. No source describes a procedure for legal gender recognition, entry-refusal grounds for foreign LGBT nationals, or whether hotel-level refusal of same-sex couples persists after the 2022 commitments.
